paragraphs.heading: An eruption that named a type
paragraphs.text: Mount Vesuvius is a stratovolcano in Campania, Italy, and it erupted in 79 AD. The event gave its name to the Vesuvian type of eruption, marked by columns of hot gases and ash that climb into the stratosphere. It also included pyroclastic flows, which are associated with Peléan eruptions.

paragraphs.heading: Warnings nobody read
paragraphs.text: On February 5, 62 AD, a major earthquake did widespread damage around the Bay of Naples, and Pompeii was hit especially hard. Some of that damage was still unrepaired when the volcano erupted in 79 AD. In the four days before the eruption there were reports of minor earthquakes, but nobody recognised them as warnings. People living around Vesuvius were used to small tremors. Pliny the Younger explained that the tremors caused no particular alarm, since Campania has them often.

paragraphs.heading: The first day
paragraphs.text: The eruption lasted two days. In the early afternoon Vesuvius erupted violently and sent a column high into the air. Ash and pumice began falling from it, blanketing the area and making roofs collapse. Rescues and escapes took place over the next few hours. One or more major earthquakes also struck at this time, bringing down walls and killing some refugees, and a mild tsunami in the bay came with them.

paragraphs.heading: The flows
paragraphs.text: Pyroclastic flows began close to the volcano at some point during the night or early on the following day. The first one left a few centimetres of ash but did no major damage. A second pyroclastic flow came in the early morning, and it was fast, dense and very hot. It knocked down many walls in its path and burned or suffocated the people who remained.

paragraphs.heading: The eyewitness
paragraphs.text: Pliny the Younger saw the event himself from the town of Misenum, which lies 29 km from Vesuvius on the far side of the Bay of Naples. His two letters preserve a detailed firsthand account, and they are the only written testimony that survives. By his description, the morning before the eruption was a normal one. Misenum was little affected on the first day. His letter never mentions Pompeii.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the ash layers
paragraphs.text: In 1982 Sigurðsson, Cashdollar and Sparks published a detailed study of the ash layers, based on excavations and surveys. Their conclusion was that the eruption had two phases, called Vesuvian and Pelean, and that these took turns six times. A first Plinian phase threw volcanic debris and hot gases up in a column, somewhere between 15 km and 30 km high, into the stratosphere. That phase lasted 18 to 20 hours and laid down a 2.8 m layer of pumice and ash to the south, towards Pompeii. The Pelean phase that followed produced pyroclastic surges, and these travelled west as far as Misenum.

paragraphs.heading: What the ash kept
paragraphs.text: A thick layer of ash from this flow sealed many bodies in cavities, and the cavities kept the shapes of the bodies. This later allowed plaster casts, a method devised by Giuseppe Fiorelli. At Pompeii and Herculaneum, the remains of more than 1,500 people have been found. The total death toll from the eruption is still unknown.
